extracted.intended_audience: historians of science, bibliographers, and informed general readers interested in Thomas Hariot and early modern scientific authorship
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing authorship, authenticity, and the evidentiary value of manuscripts, printed works, and correspondence in a biographical/historical study of an early-modern scientist. Focuses on how to judge claims about contributions, authenticity, and intellectual influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability/time/access/opportunity as attribution criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that a person assisted or authored a work should be tested against whether they had the ability, time, access, and opportunity to perform the required labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the text: 'It may well be questioned if any one of them possessed either the ability, the time, the access to the Tower, or the opportunity to perform such herculean labors of love.' The author uses these factors to argue for or against alleged assistants (Ben Jonson, Burhill, Hoskins) and to support Hariot's role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary manuscript provenance and handwriting as proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of manuscripts 'in his own handwriting' and their custody/location are taken as strong evidence of authorship and contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording and examples: 'The Hariot manuscripts, of which there are thousands of folio pages all in his own handwriting... For proof of this assertion ... the Hariot papers still preserved partly at Petworth and partly in the British Museum.' The page treats surviving papers and their provenance as key proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newly produced documents can decisively change interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduction of previously unseen primary documents (e.g., a will) can 'let in a flood of light' and dispel misconceptions about authorship or influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'The Will now first produced lets in a flood of light on the history of these valued papers, and dispels a great deal of the heaps of foreign pretension, domestic assertion, and mixed charlatanism...'. The guidance is to weigh new primary sources heavily when they appear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handwriting/material/ink/pen analysis to detect additions or authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine handwriting style, tense, pen and ink, paper dimensions and condition to decide if a document is contemporary, has multiple hands, or contains later interpolations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to the 'Note of Remembrance': 'There is a little confusion of the tenses... the last two lines... may have been added by Hariot afterwards... they are in the same handwriting, and apparently were written with the same pen and ink.' Also: note paper size and hurried penning: 'about twelve inches long and nearly four inches wide... hurriedly penned with a blunt quill'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with eyewitness/reported accounts as corroboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the document's content and order with contemporary eyewitness reports; substantial agreement (even if order varies) argues for authenticity or contemporaneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Every paragraph of the speech is noted, but not quite in the order of the speech as variously reported by those who witnessed the execution... This argues in favor of its being a note prepared beforehand.' Use discrepancies thoughtfully: close but not exact matches can support authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronological/temporal plausibility for dating documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Use known external dates/events (e.g., the time the execution was ordered) to assess when a document must have been written and whether its dating is plausible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'If so it must have been written shortly before the speech, because the order for the execution was not given in the King’s Bench Court till the afternoon of the 28th, and the execution was fixed for early the next morning.' Temporal context constrains interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bibliographic/physical description of printed works as evaluative evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed bibliographic data (full title, publisher, pagination, preface, errata, surviving copies in royal or museum collections) are used to evaluate the publication history, authenticity, and reception of a work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page gives a careful imprint for Artis Analyticae Praxis (title, publisher, year, preface pages, text pages, errata) and notes 'In the British Museum, 529 m 8, is Charles the First’s copy.' Such particulars are treated as evidence in bibliographical judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning against over-relying on a single printed work for reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: A scholar’s reputation should not be allowed to rest solely on one printed work; bibliographical and contextual investigation may alter assessments of importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'A great deal of misconception has hitherto prevailed respecting Hariot’s great printed work on Algebra. His reputation as a mathematician has been permitted to hinge chiefly upon it, very much to his disadvantage.' Use broader corpus and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of textual content (citations/passages) to assess beliefs or influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessing someone's religious or philosophical stance should be based on the presence/absence of relevant textual citations and passages in their writings or in works they influenced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Let any one notice the numerous citations of the various books of the Bible in Raleigh’s History, and he will surely fail to discover any evidence of Raleigh’s being a Deist, or that Hariot had taught him to undervalue the scripture.' So examine internal textual evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript 'waste' and marginalia can contain substantive evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Discarded notes, jottings, abstracts, and marginalia in manuscript 'waste' can contain material that materially alters understanding of authorship and contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes Hariot had directed that the 'waste' should be weeded out and destroyed, but 'this duty seems, fortunately for us, to have been neglected... among this 'waste' one has even now no great difficulty in recognizing... many jottings in chronology, geography and science.' Treat apparently minor scraps as potentially significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-referencing correspondence and contemporary networks
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess influence, priority, and access by examining correspondence and documented contacts with contemporaries (e.g., Kepler, Galileo, Lower, Protheroe).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'He was in correspondence with Kepler, and probably with Galileo. He was easily the chief of astronomers in England, and is known to have possessed the earliest books of Galileo and to have sent them to his disciples, Lower and Protheroe.' Letters and exchanges help situate claims of discovery and influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Call for competent, scientific scholarly scrutiny of new materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Newly printed or discovered materials should attract and be subjected to careful, competent, 'scientific' historical scrutiny by qualified historians before firm conclusions are drawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'The dawn however is coming, when these new materials now first printed by the Hercules Club, but not worked up, may attract the attention of some historian competent to give them a thorough scientific scrutiny and ‘pen their doctrine.’' Emphasizes expert, methodical investigation.
